q: A bus travels 30 km in the first hour and 50 km in the next hour along a straight road. What is its average speed over the two hours?
why: Average speed = total distance / total time = (30 + 50) km / 2 h = 40 km/h. Do not add the speeds or divide by only one hour.
style: Exams give two stages of a journey and ask for the average, testing whether you use total distance over total time.

q: On a distance-time graph, the line for a toy car is perfectly horizontal for 10 seconds. What is the toy car doing during this time?

opts.t: It is moving with constant speed

why: A horizontal line means the distance does not change with time, so the car is not moving. A sloping straight line would mean constant speed.
style: Exams describe the shape of a graph in words and ask what motion it represents.

q: A car starts from rest. Its speed-time graph is a straight line rising to 20 m/s at 5 s. How far does the car travel in these 5 seconds?
why: Distance equals the area under a speed-time graph. The area is a triangle: 1/2 x 5 s x 20 m/s = 50 m. Using base x height gives 100 m, which is the common slip.
style: Exams ask for distance from a graph by using the area under the line, not the slope.

q: A coin rests on a card placed over a glass. When the card is flicked away sharply sideways, the coin drops into the glass. Why does the coin not move sideways with the card?

opts.t: The card pulls the coin straight downwards
Air pushes the coin down into the glass
The coin becomes heavier when the card moves
The coin tends to stay at rest because of its inertia

why: By Newton's first law, a body at rest stays at rest unless a net force acts on it. The quick flick gives the coin almost no sideways push, so it falls straight down.
style: Exams give a small demonstration and ask which law or idea explains the surprising result.

q: A 2 kg block on a smooth table is pushed by a net force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?
why: Using F = ma, a = F/m = 10 N / 2 kg = 5 m/s^2.
style: Exams give a force and a mass and ask for the acceleration in one step.

q: A person steps from a small boat onto the river bank. The boat drifts backwards, away from the bank. Which statement best explains this?

opts.t: The boat is lighter than the person, so it moves on its own
The foot pushes the boat backwards and the boat pushes the foot forwards with an equal force
Water pushes the boat backwards when a person leaves it
The person's weight decreases, so the boat is released

why: Forces come in equal and opposite pairs. As the person pushes backwards on the boat to move forwards, the boat gets an equal push backwards.
style: Exams give an everyday situation and ask you to identify the action-reaction pair.

q: Why is sand sprinkled on a slippery floor to help people walk safely?

opts.t: It reduces the weight of the person
It increases friction between shoes and the floor
It reduces the force of gravity

why: Rough sand grains increase friction, so the shoe grips the floor and is less likely to slide.
style: Exams ask which practical step increases or reduces friction and why.

q: A person weighing 600 N stands on both feet. The total area of the two soles in contact with the floor is 0.04 m^2. What pressure does the person exert on the floor?
why: Pressure = force / area = 600 N / 0.04 m^2 = 15000 Pa. If the person stood on one foot (0.02 m^2), the pressure would double.
style: Exams give a weight and a contact area and ask for pressure, often with a follow-up on standing on one foot.

q: Why does a sharp knife cut vegetables more easily than a blunt one when the same force is applied?

opts.t: The sharp edge has a smaller area, so it exerts more pressure
The sharp edge has a larger area, so the force becomes larger
A sharp knife is always heavier than a blunt knife
A sharp edge reduces gravity on the vegetable

why: Pressure = force / area. For the same force, a smaller area gives a larger pressure, which cuts the material.
style: Exams ask you to link everyday tools to the pressure formula.

q: An iron nail sinks in water, but a huge iron ship floats. Which reason is correct?

opts.t: Iron becomes lighter when it is shaped into a ship
The ship's hollow shape displaces a large volume of water, giving an upthrust equal to its weight
The sea water pulls the ship upward because of salt
The ship's engine keeps pushing it up continuously

why: A body floats when the water it displaces weighs as much as the body. The hollow hull makes the average density of the ship less than that of water.
style: Exams contrast two objects of the same material and ask what decides floating or sinking.

q: A solid block of mass 0.5 kg has a volume of 1000 cm^3 (0.001 m^3). It is placed in water of density 1000 kg/m^3. What happens?

opts.t: It floats with one-fourth of its volume under water
It floats with half its volume under water
It floats with its whole volume just under the surface

why: Density of block = 0.5 / 0.001 = 500 kg/m^3, which is less than water, so it floats. Fraction submerged = 500 / 1000 = 1/2.
style: Exams give mass and volume, ask you to find density first, then predict floating and the submerged fraction.

q: Take g = 10 N/kg and the density of water as 1000 kg/m^3. By how much does the pressure in a lake increase at a depth of 10 m compared with the surface?
why: Extra pressure = depth x density x g = 10 m x 1000 kg/m^3 x 10 N/kg = 100000 Pa.
style: Exams ask for the pressure due to a liquid column using height, density and g.

q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror so that it makes an angle of 30 degrees with the surface of the mirror. What is the angle of reflection?
why: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal. The normal is 90 degrees from the surface, so the angle of incidence is 90 - 30 = 60 degrees, and the angle of reflection is also 60 degrees.
style: Exams give the angle with the mirror, not with the normal, to see if you convert first.

topic: Physics: image in a plane mirror
q: A girl stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. She then walks 1 m towards the mirror. What is the distance between her and her image now?
why: A plane mirror forms an image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. After walking, she is 1 m from the mirror and her image is 1 m behind it, so the gap is 1 + 1 = 2 m.
style: Exams ask for the object-to-image distance after the object moves, not the distance to the mirror.

q: A straw dipped in a glass of water looks bent at the water surface. What causes this?

opts.t: The straw really bends in water
Light changes direction when it passes from water to air
The glass reflects the straw twice

why: Light travels at different speeds in water and air, so it bends (refracts) at the boundary, and the straw appears to bend.
style: Exams describe an everyday optical illusion and ask for the cause.

q: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block at a slant. Which statement is correct?

opts.t: It bends away from the normal because light travels faster in glass
It does not bend because glass is transparent
It bends towards the normal because light travels faster in glass
It bends towards the normal because light travels more slowly in glass

why: Glass is optically denser than air, so light slows down on entering it and bends towards the normal.
style: Exams ask for both the direction of bending and the reason, so that guessing one half fails.

topic: Physics: convex lens as a magnifier
q: A convex lens is used as a magnifying glass to read small print. How must the print be placed, and what kind of image is seen?

opts.t: Within the focal length; a virtual, upright and enlarged image
Beyond twice the focal length; a real, inverted and smaller image
At the focal length; a real image formed at infinity
Between f and 2f; a virtual and diminished image

why: When the object is closer than the focal length, a convex lens forms a virtual, upright, magnified image on the same side as the object.
style: Exams give a use of a lens and ask for the object position and image nature together.

q: Astronauts on the Moon talk to each other through radios even when they stand close together. What is the reason?

opts.t: The Moon's gravity is too weak for people to speak
Sound cannot travel through the vacuum around them, but radio waves can
Their helmets make sound louder than light
Radios make sound travel faster than light

why: Sound needs a material medium such as air. The Moon has almost no air, while radio waves can travel through a vacuum.
style: Exams ask why a natural method fails in space and what replaces it.

q: A girl claps near a cliff and hears the echo 2 s later. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, how far away is the cliff?
why: In 2 s the sound travels 340 x 2 = 680 m, which is the journey to the cliff and back. The cliff is half of that: 340 m.
style: Exams test whether you remember that the echo covers the distance twice.

q: The hum of a mosquito sounds shriller than the roar of a lion. Which property of the mosquito's sound is greater?
why: A shriller sound has a higher pitch, and pitch depends on frequency. Loudness depends on amplitude, and the speed in air is the same for both sounds.
style: Exams ask you to connect a sound described in everyday words to a wave property.

q: On a sunny afternoon at the coast, a cool breeze blows from the sea towards the land. Why?

opts.t: Air above hot land rises, and cooler air from the sea moves in to replace it
Water vapour from the sea pushes air onto the land
The sea is hotter than the land, so air flows to the land
The land attracts the air by gravity more than the sea does

why: Land heats faster than water. Warm air over land rises, leaving low pressure, and cooler sea air flows in. This is a convection current.
style: Exams give a natural phenomenon and ask you to explain it through heat flow.

q: Using K = degrees C + 273, what is a temperature of 50 degrees C on the Kelvin scale?
why: K = 50 + 273 = 323 K. The Kelvin scale starts from absolute zero, so there are no negative values.
style: Exams ask for a quick conversion between temperature scales.

q: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 degrees C? The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/(kg degree C).
why: Q = m x c x change in temperature = 2 x 4200 x 10 = 84000 J.
style: Exams give mass, specific heat and temperature change and ask for the heat in joules.

q: Two identical bulbs are connected in series with one cell. One bulb is unscrewed from its holder. What happens to the other bulb?

opts.t: It glows dimmer but stays on
It goes off because the circuit is broken

why: In a series circuit there is only one path for the current. Removing one bulb breaks the circuit, so the other bulb also goes off.
style: Exams ask you to predict what changes when one component is removed from a circuit.

q: A potential difference of 6 V is applied across a resistor of 12 ohm. What current flows through it?
style: Exams ask for a single application of V = IR.

q: A 100 W bulb is switched on for 5 hours. How many units (kWh) of electrical energy does it use?
why: Energy = power x time = 0.1 kW x 5 h = 0.5 kWh. One unit is one kilowatt-hour, so remember to convert watts to kilowatts.
style: Exams ask for electricity-bill units and trap students who forget to convert W into kW.

q: A bar magnet is broken into two equal pieces. What do you find?

opts.t: One piece has only a north pole and the other only a south pole
Each piece is a magnet with its own north and south pole
Each piece has two north poles

why: Poles cannot be separated. Breaking a magnet gives two smaller magnets, each with both a north and a south pole.
style: Exams give an action on a magnet and ask you to predict what you observe.

q: A person pushes hard with a force of 200 N on a large wall, but the wall does not move. How much work does the person do on the wall?

opts.t: 200 J, because the force is 200 N
Slightly more than 200 J, because the wall resists
It cannot be found unless the time is given
0 J, because the wall has no displacement

why: Work = force x displacement in the direction of force. With no displacement, the work done on the wall is zero, however large the force.
style: Exams check that you know work in science needs movement, not just effort.

q: A motor lifts a 200 kg load through 15 m in 20 s at a steady speed. Take g = 10 N/kg. What power does it deliver to the load?
why: Work = m x g x h = 200 x 10 x 15 = 30000 J. Power = work / time = 30000 / 20 = 1500 W.
style: Exams combine work, g and time in a single question and check each step.

q: A ball of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m/s has kinetic energy 9 J. What is its kinetic energy if its speed is doubled to 6 m/s?
why: Kinetic energy = 1/2 x m x v^2. Doubling v multiplies it by 2^2 = 4, so 9 x 4 = 36 J. Check: 1/2 x 2 x 36 = 36 J.
style: Exams ask how an energy changes when a quantity is doubled, to test the square relation.

q: Naphthalene balls kept in a cupboard become smaller over several weeks without leaving any liquid behind. What is this process called?
why: In sublimation, a solid changes directly into a gas without passing through the liquid state.
style: Exams describe an observation and ask you to name the change of state.

q: A large amount of cooking gas is stored in a small LPG cylinder. What property of gas particles makes this possible?

opts.t: Gas particles are very heavy and stay close together
Gas particles attract each other strongly like in a solid
There are large spaces between gas particles, so gas can be compressed

why: Particles in a gas are far apart with a lot of empty space, so pressure can squeeze them into a much smaller volume.
style: Exams link an everyday use to the particle model of matter.

q: Water in an earthen pot (matka) stays cooler than the surroundings in summer. What is the main reason?

opts.t: Water seeping through pores evaporates and takes heat from the pot and the water
Clay is a perfect heat insulator
The pot makes new cold water

why: Evaporation needs heat, which is taken from the water and the pot, so they cool down.
style: Exams ask you to explain a daily cooling phenomenon through evaporation.

q: A pressure cooker cooks dal faster than an open pan. What is the main reason?

opts.t: Higher pressure lowers the boiling point of water
Higher pressure raises the boiling point, so water gets hotter than 100 degrees C
The lid makes the flame hotter
Steam has no heat, so the food cooks by pressure alone

why: Inside a closed cooker, pressure rises, so water boils at a higher temperature. Hotter water cooks the food faster.
style: Exams ask which factor changes when a household appliance works and why that speeds a process.

q: Which sequence correctly separates a mixture of salt and sand?

opts.t: Filter the dry mixture, then add water
Add water and stir, filter, then evaporate the filtrate
Add water, then use a magnet

why: Salt dissolves in water but sand does not. Filtering removes the sand, and evaporating the clear solution leaves the salt.
style: Exams give a mixture and ask for the correct order of separation steps.

q: Which method is best to separate iron filings from sulphur powder?
why: Iron is attracted by a magnet and sulphur is not. This property is used for the separation.
style: Exams ask you to pick the method that uses a property in which the two components differ.

q: A pinch of baking soda is added to sour dhokla batter before steaming, and the dhokla turns soft and spongy. Why?

opts.t: Baking soda reacts with the acid and heat to release carbon dioxide gas that gets trapped
Baking soda releases oxygen that burns the batter
Baking soda turns into water vapour only
Baking soda makes the batter denser

why: Sodium hydrogencarbonate gives carbon dioxide on reacting with acid or on heating. The gas bubbles make the dhokla spongy.
style: Exams use a cooking example and ask you to identify the gas formed and its effect.

q: A drop of black ink on filter paper is dipped in water, and the ink splits into several coloured bands. Why?

opts.t: All dyes are the same, so they disappear in the water
Different dyes dissolve and move upwards at different rates
Water changes the dyes into new colours by burning
The paper adds the colours to the ink

why: The dyes in black ink differ in how well they dissolve and cling to paper, so they travel different distances. This is chromatography.
style: Exams show a separation technique and ask what property makes it work.

q: A mixture of ethanol (boiling point 78 degrees C) and water (100 degrees C) is heated slowly in a distillation set-up. What comes over first?

opts.t: Mainly water, because it is more common
Both equally, because they are miscible
Mainly ethanol, because it boils at a lower temperature
Neither, because they cannot be separated

why: Distillation separates miscible liquids with different boiling points. The one with the lower boiling point vaporises first and is collected first.
style: Exams give boiling points and ask which liquid is collected first.

q: Which of the following is a chemical change?
why: In souring, new substances such as lactic acid are formed and cannot be turned back easily. The others change only the form or state, not the substance.
style: Exams give four everyday changes and ask for the one that forms a new substance.

q: Which observation is the strongest evidence that a chemical change has taken place?

opts.t: A silvery metal ribbon burns with a bright white flame and leaves a white powder
A wire glows and gets hot when current flows through it
A solid disappears when it is stirred into water
A block of ice becomes a puddle of water

why: A new substance, a white powder, forms and cannot go back to the metal ribbon by cooling. Glowing and heating of a wire is physical, since the wire is unchanged afterwards.
style: Exams include a tempting distractor such as light or heat that also appears in physical changes.

q: A few drops of lemon juice are added to blue litmus solution. What do you observe?
why: Lemon juice contains citric acid. Acids turn blue litmus red.
style: Exams ask for the colour change of an indicator in an everyday acid or base.

q: A yellow turmeric stain on a white shirt turns reddish-brown when soap is rubbed on it. What does this show?

opts.t: The shirt is made of acid

why: Turmeric is a natural indicator that turns reddish-brown in bases. Soap solution is basic.
style: Exams ask you to infer the nature of a substance from the colour change of a natural indicator.

q: Why is milk of magnesia taken to relieve acidity in the stomach?

opts.t: It is a strong acid that makes the stomach empty
It is an indicator that shows the acid
It heats the stomach and removes the acid
It is a mild base that neutralises the excess acid

why: Acid indigestion is caused by too much hydrochloric acid. A mild base neutralises it, forming salt and water.
style: Exams link neutralisation to everyday health.

q: Solution X has pH 3 and solution Y has pH 5. How do their hydrogen ion concentrations compare?

opts.t: X has 100 times higher hydrogen ion concentration than Y
X has 2 times higher concentration than Y
X has 10 times lower concentration than Y
X has 1000 times higher concentration than Y

why: Each pH unit is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration. Two units apart means 10 x 10 = 100 times, and the lower pH has the higher concentration.
style: Exams test that pH is a logarithmic scale rather than a straight scale.

q: A colourless solution turns pink when phenolphthalein is added. Which pH value is most likely for the solution?
why: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acids and neutral solutions and pink in bases, so the solution is basic, with pH above 7.
style: Exams give an indicator result and ask for the matching pH.

q: Zinc granules are added to dilute hydrochloric acid, and bubbles appear. A burning splinter is brought near the mouth of the test tube. What is observed, and which gas is it?

opts.t: The splinter burns brighter; oxygen gas
The splinter goes out; carbon dioxide gas

why: Metals such as zinc react with dilute acids to give hydrogen gas. Hydrogen burns with a pop sound.
style: Exams give a reaction and a test and ask you to match the gas.

q: Which of these metals can displace copper from copper sulphate solution?
why: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution. Iron is more reactive than copper, while silver, gold and mercury are less reactive.
style: Exams use the reactivity series to predict whether a displacement reaction occurs.

q: Copper is widely used to make electrical wires. Which pair of properties makes it suitable?

opts.t: It is a good conductor of electricity and it is ductile
It is brittle and a poor conductor
It is a good insulator and malleable

why: Wires need to conduct electricity well and to be drawn into thin wires, which means being ductile.
style: Exams link a use to the right pair of properties.

q: Four identical iron nails are kept in different conditions. Which nail will rust the most?

opts.t: The nail in dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride
The nail in tap water in an open test tube
The nail in boiled water covered by a layer of oil
The nail coated with grease kept in dry air

why: Rusting needs both oxygen and water. Only the nail in open tap water gets both. Dry air has no moisture, boiled water with oil has no oxygen, and grease keeps both away.
style: Exams show several set-ups and ask which satisfies all the conditions for a process.

q: Iron sheets coated with zinc (galvanised iron) do not rust even when the coating is scratched and iron is exposed. Why?

opts.t: Zinc is less reactive than iron, so it is never attacked
Scratches get sealed by iron oxide immediately
Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it reacts first and protects the iron
Zinc coating makes the iron stronger by heating

why: Zinc gives up electrons more easily than iron, so it corrodes in preference to the iron.
style: Exams ask why a protection method still works when the coating is damaged.

q: Air contains about 21 percent oxygen by volume. How much oxygen is present in 200 litres of air?
why: Oxygen volume = 21/100 x 200 = 42 litres. The 156 litres is about the amount of nitrogen (78 percent), not oxygen.
style: Exams give a percentage composition and ask for the amount in a given volume.

q: Why is water not used to put out a fire in cooking oil?

opts.t: Oil is lighter than water, so it floats and spreads the burning
Water is a fuel for oil fires
Oil dissolves in water and burns underwater
Water cannot take heat from burning oil

why: Oil does not mix with water and floats on it. The burning oil can spread on top of the water instead of being cooled and covered.
style: Exams ask you to choose a method and justify it using properties of the substances.

q: Hard water gives very little lather with soap and leaves a white scum. What is the reason?

opts.t: Hard water contains too much chlorine, which removes soap
Calcium and magnesium ions in the water react with soap to form scum
Hard water is acidic and turns soap into acid
Hard water has no dissolved substances

why: Soap reacts with calcium and magnesium ions to form an insoluble scum. Lather forms only after these ions are used up.
style: Exams ask for the cause of an everyday observation in a washing situation.

q: How many atoms are present in one molecule of sulphuric acid, H2SO4?
why: Add the subscripts: 2 hydrogen + 1 sulphur + 4 oxygen = 7 atoms.
style: Exams ask you to count atoms from a formula.

q: A neutral atom of sodium has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. How many electrons does it have, and what is its mass number?
why: A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons, so 11 electrons. Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23.
style: Exams give the particle counts and ask for atomic quantities.

q: The formula of chalk is CaCO3. Using Ca = 40, C = 12 and O = 16, what is the mass of 0.5 mole of CaCO3?
why: Molar mass of CaCO3 = 40 + 12 + 3 x 16 = 100 g/mol. Mass of 0.5 mole = 0.5 x 100 = 50 g.
style: Exams first ask for the molar mass and then for the mass of a fraction of a mole.

q: 6 g of carbon burns completely in oxygen and forms 22 g of carbon dioxide. What mass of oxygen was used?
why: By the law of conservation of mass, mass of reactants = mass of products. Oxygen used = 22 - 6 = 16 g.
style: Exams use this law to find a missing mass in a reaction.

q: Which of these compounds is a hydrocarbon?
why: A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen. The other compounds also contain oxygen.
style: Exams give formulae and ask you to classify them.

q: How does soap help to remove oil and grease from a dirty cloth?

opts.t: Soap burns the grease into carbon dioxide
Soap makes oil dissolve into water as a true solution
Soap makes the cloth repel water completely
One end of the soap molecule sticks to oil and the other end to water, so oil is lifted away

why: Soap molecules have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail. They surround the grease as tiny droplets that are washed away with water.
style: Exams ask for the mechanism of cleaning rather than just the word 'detergent'.

q: In the human heart, which chamber receives oxygen-rich blood coming back from the lungs?
why: Blood loaded with oxygen in the lungs returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. It then passes to the left ventricle, which pumps it to the body. The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the body.
style: A competitive exam gives a labelled flow of blood and asks which chamber or vessel carries oxygen-rich or oxygen-poor blood.

q: Which pair of substances do green leaves take in to make food by photosynthesis?
why: Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air through stomata and water from the roots. With sunlight and chlorophyll they make glucose and release oxygen.
style: The exam asks you to separate the inputs of photosynthesis from its products.

q: In the food chain grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake, grass holds 10,000 kJ of usable energy. Only about 10 percent of the energy at one level passes to the next level. How much reaches the snake?
why: Grass 10,000 kJ; grasshopper 10 percent of that = 1,000 kJ; frog = 100 kJ; snake = 10 kJ. Three transfers, so 10,000 x 0.1 x 0.1 x 0.1 = 10 kJ. This is why food chains are short.
style: A numerical energy-pyramid question using the 10 percent rule, with the trap of counting the wrong number of steps.

q: In which part of the human digestive system is most of the digested food absorbed into the blood?
why: The small intestine is long and its inner wall has finger-like villi that give a very large surface area and a rich blood supply, so digested nutrients pass quickly into the blood. The large intestine mainly absorbs water.
style: A direct recall question linking structure (villi) to function (absorption).

q: Why does India have different seasons such as summer and winter?

opts.t: Earth's axis is tilted, so sunlight falls more directly on each hemisphere at different times of the year
Earth is much nearer the Sun in summer and much farther in winter
The Sun gives out more heat in some months than in others
Earth spins faster in summer than in winter

why: The 23.5 degree tilt of Earth's axis changes how directly sunlight strikes a place and how long the day lasts. In fact Earth is slightly nearer the Sun in early January, so distance is not the cause.
style: Exams test the common misconception that seasons come from distance to the Sun.

topic: Earth: Rocks and the rock cycle
q: Marble is formed when limestone is changed by heat and pressure deep inside the Earth. To which group of rocks does marble belong?
why: Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks changed by heat and pressure without melting completely. Limestone is sedimentary; when changed it becomes marble.
style: A classification question that asks you to name the rock type from how it forms.

q: Paddy fields in many Indian river plains are on clayey soil. Which property of clay suits rice?

opts.t: Its large particles let water drain away quickly
It is full of big air spaces that keep roots dry
Its very fine particles leave tiny gaps, so it holds water for a long time
It contains no minerals, so weeds cannot grow

why: Clay particles are extremely small and packed closely, so water moves through slowly and is held. Rice needs standing water, so such soil is ideal. Sandy soil drains fast and suits crops needing less water.
style: The exam links a soil property (particle size) to a crop need.

q: A girl feels tired and looks pale, and her blood test shows low haemoglobin. Which change in her meals would help most?

opts.t: Adding more sugar and white rice
Adding iron-rich foods such as spinach, jaggery and pulses

why: Haemoglobin contains iron, and low iron causes anaemia. Green leafy vegetables, jaggery and pulses supply iron, and vitamin C helps the body absorb it.
style: A short real-life case in which you choose the nutrient that fixes the problem.

q: Which planet takes the least time to go once around the Sun?
why: The planet closest to the Sun has the shortest orbit and moves fastest. Mercury completes a year in about 88 Earth days.
style: An ordering question: closer planets have shorter years.

q: On a sunny afternoon at a coastal town like Puri, a cool wind blows from the sea towards the land. What explains this?

opts.t: Sea heats faster than land, so air flows from land to sea
Land heats faster than sea, so warm air rises over land and cooler sea air moves in to replace it
Land stays cooler, so cold air from land pushes towards the sea
Earth's rotation alone pushes air towards the land, whatever the temperature

why: Land has a lower specific heat than water, so it warms faster in daytime. Air above it becomes warm and light and rises. The cooler, denser air over the sea flows in as the sea breeze.
style: A cause-and-effect reasoning question on convection in the atmosphere.

q: What happens in the chest when you breathe in?

opts.t: The diaphragm relaxes and moves up, pushing air into the lungs
The ribs move down and in, so the chest volume increases
The diaphragm contracts and moves down, the chest volume increases and air pressure inside falls, so air rushes in
The lungs contract with their own muscles and pull air in

why: Air flows from higher to lower pressure. The diaphragm moves down and the ribs move up and out, increasing chest volume. Pressure inside drops below outside pressure and air enters. Lungs have no muscles of their own.
style: The exam tests the pressure and volume explanation rather than just the word 'inhale'.

q: A pesticide that does not break down is sprayed on a farm. It passes along the chain crop -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> eagle. In which organism will its concentration be highest?
why: A non-degradable chemical is stored in body tissue. Each animal eats many organisms from the level below, so the chemical builds up at each step (biomagnification). The top carnivore ends up with the highest amount.
style: A food-chain reasoning question about how pollutants build up at higher levels.

q: Which part of the atmosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet rays?

opts.t: The ozone layer in the stratosphere
The layer of clouds near the ground
The oxygen present near sea level
The layer of carbon dioxide that traps heat

why: Ozone (O3) high in the stratosphere absorbs most UV-B and UV-C rays. Chemicals such as CFCs destroy ozone, so their use has been reduced worldwide.
style: A recall item that connects a layer of the atmosphere with its protective role.

q: Which of these is NOT a greenhouse gas?
why: Greenhouse gases absorb heat radiated by Earth. Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour do this. Nitrogen, which makes up about 78 percent of air, does not.
style: An 'odd one out' question on atmospheric gases.

q: Which weather condition makes a leafy plant lose water through its leaves fastest?

opts.t: A cool, humid and calm day
A cold, cloudy and windy day
A hot, dry and windy day
A warm, very humid and calm day

why: Transpiration speeds up when it is warm (more evaporation), when the air is dry (steeper vapour gradient) and when wind removes the moist air near the leaf. Humid, still air slows it.
style: A question about factors that increase a rate, where you must check every factor in the option.

q: Which statement describes the climate of a place rather than its weather?

opts.t: It rained heavily in Chennai last night
Delhi reached 41 degrees C yesterday afternoon
In a typical year Chennai gets most of its rain between October and December

why: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular time. Climate is the pattern averaged over many years. A statement about what usually happens in a season is climate.
style: A classification between a short-term event and a long-term pattern.

q: When does a lunar eclipse occur?

opts.t: When Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon in a straight line, at full moon
When the Moon lies between the Sun and Earth, at new moon
When Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon, at new moon
When Venus passes between the Sun and the Moon

why: In a lunar eclipse Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. This needs the Sun, Earth and Moon in a line with Earth in the middle, which happens only at full moon. The Moon between Sun and Earth gives a solar eclipse at new moon.
style: A positional-reasoning question that tests both the line-up and the phase.

q: A resting adult's heart beats 72 times per minute and pumps 70 mL of blood at each beat. How much blood does the heart pump in one hour?
why: Per minute: 72 x 70 = 5,040 mL. Per hour: 5,040 x 60 = 302,400 mL = 302.4 L, which is about 302 litres. The 5 L figure is only one minute's output.
style: A unit-conversion calculation set in a biological context.

q: What is the role of decomposers such as bacteria and fungi in an ecosystem?

opts.t: They make food from sunlight for the whole ecosystem
They hunt herbivores to keep their numbers low
They break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil
They store energy as fat for the predators to eat

why: Decomposers feed on dead matter and wastes, releasing minerals that plants take up again. Without them dead material would pile up and nutrients would run out.
style: A role-identification question about the parts of a food web.

topic: Earth: Gravity and weight on the Moon
q: The pull of gravity on the Moon is one-sixth of that on Earth. Take g = 10 N/kg on Earth. A student of mass 60 kg goes to the Moon. What are the student's mass and weight there?
why: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change: 60 kg. Weight = mass x g. Moon g = 10/6 N/kg, so weight = 60 x 10/6 = 100 N, compared with 600 N on Earth.
style: Tests the difference between mass and weight with a simple calculation.

q: A meal has 50 g of carbohydrate, 20 g of protein and 10 g of fat. Carbohydrate and protein give 17 kJ per gram and fat gives 37 kJ per gram. How much energy does the meal give?
why: Carbohydrate: 50 x 17 = 850 kJ. Protein: 20 x 17 = 340 kJ. Fat: 10 x 37 = 370 kJ. Total = 850 + 340 + 370 = 1,560 kJ. Fat gives more than twice the energy per gram.
style: A multi-step table-reading calculation with a trap if one value is used for all components.

q: Why does the windward side of the Western Ghats get very heavy rain in the south-west monsoon?

opts.t: Dry desert winds pick up moisture as they sink down the slopes
Moist air from the Arabian Sea is forced up the slopes, cools, and its water vapour condenses
The mountains heat the air and turn it into water vapour
Air sinks and warms on the slopes, which forms thick clouds

why: Rising air expands and cools. Cool air holds less water vapour, so the vapour condenses into clouds and rain on the windward side. The leeward side lies in a rain shadow and is drier.
style: A cause-and-effect geography-science question about relief rainfall.

q: A plant with leaves that have green and white patches is kept in sunlight. One leaf is boiled in alcohol to remove its colour and then iodine is dropped on it. Which result and conclusion are correct?

opts.t: Only the white parts turn blue-black, showing that white tissue stores starch
The whole leaf turns blue-black, showing that starch is made everywhere
Only the green parts turn blue-black, showing that chlorophyll is needed to make starch
No part turns blue-black, because iodine tests only for sugar

why: Iodine turns blue-black in the presence of starch. Starch is made only where chlorophyll and light are present, so only the green patches react. The white patches have no chlorophyll.
style: An experiment-interpretation question: read the result and state what it proves.

q: A geologist wants to search for fossils. Which rock is the best place to look?
why: Fossils are preserved in sedimentary rocks, which form in layers from sediments that bury dead organisms. Granite and basalt form from molten rock, and quartzite is metamorphic, so their heat would destroy fossils.
style: A classification question that links rock formation with fossil preservation.

topic: Mechanisms: Levers of the second class
q: A wheelbarrow has its wheel at the front, the load in the middle of the barrow and the handles at the back, where you lift. To which class of lever does it belong?

opts.t: Second class, with the load between the fulcrum and the effort
First class, with the fulcrum between the load and the effort
Third class, with the effort between the fulcrum and the load
It is not a lever at all

why: The wheel axle is the fulcrum. The load sits between the wheel and the handles, where you apply the effort. The load is between fulcrum and effort, so it is second class, and the effort is smaller than the load.
style: The question shows a familiar tool and asks you to place the fulcrum, load and effort.

topic: Mechanisms: Levers of the third class
q: Which of these is a third-class lever, with the effort applied between the fulcrum and the load?

opts.t: Claw hammer pulling out a nail

why: In tweezers the joint at the end is the fulcrum, your fingers press in the middle and the tips hold the load, so the effort is between the two. Scissors and a claw hammer are first class and a nutcracker is second class.
style: A classification of everyday tools into the three lever classes.

q: A crowbar rests on a stone that acts as the fulcrum. A rock presses on the bar 0.3 m from the stone. A worker pushes at 1.2 m from the stone on the other side. If the rock resists with 400 N, what is the least effort needed?
why: Principle of moments: effort x effort arm = load x load arm. Effort x 1.2 = 400 x 0.3 = 120, so effort = 120/1.2 = 100 N. The mechanical advantage is 1.2/0.3 = 4.
style: A moments calculation, with the wrong answers made by swapping the two arms.

q: A 40 kg child sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a 30 kg child sit on the other side to balance it?
why: Balance needs equal moments: 40 x 1.5 = 60 = 30 x d, so d = 2.0 m. The lighter child must sit farther away.
style: A balance-of-moments question with whole-number values.

topic: Mechanisms: Levers in the human body
q: When you bend your elbow to lift a heavy book in your hand, the biceps muscle pulls on the forearm close to the elbow joint. Which statement is correct?

opts.t: It is a third-class lever, so the muscle force is larger than the weight, but the hand moves a long way quickly
It is a second-class lever, so the muscle force is smaller than the weight
It is a first-class lever, with the elbow between the muscle and the hand
It is a third-class lever, so the muscle force is smaller than the weight

why: The elbow is the fulcrum, the muscle pulls near the elbow (effort) and the book is far out (load). The effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so the effort must be larger than the load. The gain is a big, fast movement of the hand.
style: A reasoning question where you must classify the lever and state its trade-off.

q: A single fixed pulley hangs from a beam above a well. Ignoring friction, what does it do?

opts.t: It changes the direction of the pull, and the effort equals the load
It doubles the distance the load moves

why: A fixed pulley is like an equal-armed lever. Pulling down raises the load, which is convenient, but the effort is the same as the load and the rope moves the same distance as the load.
style: A check of what a single pulley gives: direction, not force.

q: A pulley system has 4 rope sections supporting the moving block. It lifts an 800 N load by 1 m. Ignoring friction and the weight of the pulleys, what are the effort and the length of rope pulled?
why: Velocity ratio = 4 supporting sections. Effort = 800/4 = 200 N and the rope pulled = 4 x 1 = 4 m. Work in = 200 x 4 = 800 J = work out (800 x 1).
style: A pulley question that checks force gain against distance lost.

q: A pulley system with velocity ratio 3 needs an effort of 250 N to lift a load of 600 N. What is its efficiency?
why: Mechanical advantage = load/effort = 600/250 = 2.4. Efficiency = MA/VR = 2.4/3 = 0.8 = 80 percent. The rest of the effort goes into friction and lifting the moving pulleys.
style: A standard efficiency formula, MA divided by VR, with distractors from common slips.

q: Two gears mesh with each other. If the left gear turns clockwise, how does the right gear turn?

opts.t: Clockwise but at half the speed

why: Teeth in contact move in the same direction at the point of contact, so the two gears must rotate in opposite senses. A third gear in a row, an idler, turns the same way as the first.
style: A direction-of-rotation question on simple gear pairs.

q: A driver gear with 20 teeth turns at 120 rpm and drives a gear with 60 teeth. At what speed does the driven gear turn?
why: Gear ratio = 60/20 = 3, so the driven gear turns three times slower: 120/3 = 40 rpm. Check: teeth passing per minute are 20 x 120 = 2,400 = 60 x 40.
style: A gear-ratio calculation where the bigger gear turns slower.

q: Gear A (20 teeth) turns at 90 rpm and meshes with gear B (40 teeth), which meshes with gear C (60 teeth). B is an idler. What are the speed and direction of C compared with A?
why: An idler does not change the speed ratio, only the direction. Speed of C = 90 x 20/60 = 30 rpm. A turns one way, B the other, and C the same way as A.
style: A compound reasoning question where the idler is a distraction for speed but matters for direction.

q: A bicycle has a 48-tooth front chainwheel and a 16-tooth rear sprocket. The rear wheel has a circumference of 2 m. How far does the cycle move for one full turn of the pedals?
why: One pedal turn moves 48 chain links, so the rear sprocket turns 48/16 = 3 times. The wheel turns with the sprocket, so distance = 3 x 2 m = 6 m.
style: A chain of ratios from pedal to road, a classic aptitude type.

topic: Mechanisms: Low gear on a cycle
q: When climbing a steep slope on a geared cycle, a rider moves the chain to the largest rear sprocket. Why does this help?

opts.t: It gives a larger driving force at the wheel for each push on the pedal, at the cost of speed
It gives a higher speed for the same push, because friction is reduced
It makes the rider's weight smaller on the slope
It shortens the chain so that less work is needed

why: A large rear sprocket gives a low gear ratio: the wheel turns fewer times per pedal turn, so the force at the ground is larger. Work is not reduced, because the cycle moves less distance per pedal stroke.
style: A trade-off question: force gained is speed lost.

q: A 500 N load is pushed up a smooth ramp 5 m long to a platform 2 m high. What is the least force needed along the ramp?
why: Work on the load = 500 x 2 = 1,000 J. With no friction, effort x 5 m = 1,000 J, so effort = 200 N. Force = load x height/length = 500 x 2/5 = 200 N.
style: An energy-conservation approach to ramps.

q: Two bolts have the same diameter. One has threads 1 mm apart and the other 2 mm apart. Both are turned with the same spanner. Which statement is true?

opts.t: The 2 mm pitch bolt has the greater mechanical advantage
Both have the same mechanical advantage, since the diameter is the same
The 1 mm pitch bolt moves forward less per turn, so it has the greater mechanical advantage
The 1 mm pitch bolt moves forward more per turn, so it needs less force

why: A screw is a rolled-up ramp. A smaller pitch is a gentler ramp, so a bolt moves less per turn and the same turning effort gives a bigger force along the axis. A fine thread holds more tightly and is harder to loosen by accident.
style: A comparison question using the ramp idea for screws.

q: A steering wheel has a radius of 20 cm and the shaft it turns has a radius of 2 cm. An ideal driver pushes with 5 N at the rim. What force acts at the surface of the shaft?
why: Moments about the axis are equal: 5 x 20 = F x 2, so F = 50 N. The mechanical advantage is the ratio of radii, 20/2 = 10.
style: A torque comparison on a wheel and axle.

topic: Structures: Stability and centre of gravity
q: Which design makes a vehicle least likely to overturn on a bend?

opts.t: A low centre of gravity and a wide wheelbase
A high centre of gravity and a narrow wheelbase
A high load on the roof and wide wheels
A low centre of gravity and a very narrow wheelbase

why: An object tips when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base. A low centre of gravity and a wide base give the greatest tilt before this happens.
style: A design-judgement question about stable shapes.

q: A loaded bus tilts to one side on a slope. When will it topple over?

opts.t: When the bus has tilted by more than 45 degrees
When the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside the wheels on the lower side
When the vertical line through its centre of gravity passes through the middle of its base
When the weight of the bus is larger than the weight of the road

why: A tilted object turns back if the line of the weight still falls within the base, because the weight then gives a restoring turning effect. Once the line passes beyond the edge, weight turns it over. There is no fixed angle for every object.
style: A condition-for-toppling question that uses the vertical line through the centre of gravity.

q: A uniform box has a base 24 cm wide and its centre of gravity is 16 cm above the base, in the middle. It is tilted about one bottom edge. At about what angle of tilt will it be on the point of toppling?
why: It topples when the centre of gravity is directly above the pivot edge. The centre is 12 cm sideways from the edge and 16 cm up, so tan(angle) = 12/16 = 0.75, which is about 37 degrees. The 53 degrees option comes from inverting the ratio.
style: A geometry-based stability calculation using a 3-4-5 triangle.

q: Old stone arches in bridges and gateways stay up mainly because the stones are:

opts.t: Stretched in tension, hanging from the top stone
Glued in place so that they bend like a beam
Held up by the weight of the keystone alone
Pressed together in compression, with the load directed to the supports at the sides

why: An arch turns the downward load into a push along the curve towards its two ends (abutments). Stone resists squeezing well, so a curved shape lets it carry large loads without pulling forces.
style: Asks which type of force acts in a given structure.

q: Why are triangles used in the girders of railway bridges?

opts.t: A triangle cannot change its shape unless one side changes length, so it is rigid
A triangle uses no material at its corners
A triangle is always lighter than any other shape
A triangle looks better than a square frame

why: A frame of four bars can lean over into a parallelogram, but three bars joined by pins form a rigid shape. Trusses are triangles joined together, so each member carries only a push or a pull.
style: A why-question linking a geometric property to structural use.

q: A beam rests on two supports with a heavy load at its middle and sags slightly. What happens at its top edge and bottom edge?

opts.t: The top is stretched and the bottom is squeezed
The top is squeezed (compression) and the bottom is stretched (tension)

why: When a beam sags, its top surface becomes shorter and the bottom surface becomes longer. Between them lies a neutral layer with no stress. This is why reinforcing steel is placed near the bottom of concrete beams.
style: An identify-the-stress question for a loaded beam.

q: In a suspension bridge, which description of the main cables and the tall towers is correct?

opts.t: The cables are in compression and the towers are in tension
The cables are in tension and the towers are in compression

why: The deck hangs from the cables, so they are pulled tight and carry tension. The cables rest on the towers and push down on them, so the towers are squeezed.
style: Matches parts of a bridge with tension or compression.

q: A wooden plank 10 cm wide and 5 cm thick spans a gap. Bending stiffness is proportional to (width x depth cubed). How many times stiffer is the plank when placed on its edge (10 cm deep) than when laid flat (5 cm deep)?
why: Flat: width 10, depth 5, so 10 x 5^3 = 1,250. On edge: width 5, depth 10, so 5 x 10^3 = 5,000. Ratio = 5,000/1,250 = 4. Depth counts cubed, which is why floor joists are deep and narrow.
style: A proportional reasoning question with a power law.

q: A steel wire of cross-section area 2 mm squared carries a pull of 400 N. What is the stress in the wire?
why: Stress = force/area = 400 N / 2 mm^2 = 200 N/mm^2, which is 200 MPa. A thinner wire carries the same load with a higher stress and breaks sooner.
style: A direct stress = force/area calculation, with answers made by inverting the ratio.

q: Concrete beams are reinforced with steel rods mainly because:

opts.t: Concrete is weak when squeezed, and steel adds weight
Concrete is strong when squeezed but weak when stretched, and steel resists the pulling forces
Steel makes concrete dry faster in the sun
Steel stops water from ever touching the concrete

why: Concrete can carry large compression but cracks under small tension. The steel rods are placed where the beam is stretched and take over those pulling forces. The two materials expand at nearly the same rate with temperature, so they work well together.
style: A materials-selection question based on the strengths of each material.

q: Why does a steel ship float although steel is denser than water?

opts.t: Steel becomes lighter when it enters water
The air inside the ship changes the density of the steel itself
Its hollow shape displaces water equal in weight to the ship before it is fully under
Salt in sea water makes all steel float

why: A body floats when the weight of water it displaces equals its own weight. A hollow hull spreads the steel over a huge volume, so its average density is below that of water.
style: A why-question about displacement, with a trap about the density of the material.

q: A wooden block of mass 3 kg has a volume of 0.005 cubic metres and floats in water of density 1,000 kg per cubic metre. What fraction of its volume is under water?
why: Density of block = 3/0.005 = 600 kg/m^3. A floating body sinks to a fraction equal to density ratio: 600/1,000 = 0.6, i.e. 60 percent. Check: displaced water 0.003 m^3 x 1,000 = 3 kg.
style: A floating-body calculation using relative density.

q: A ship sails from the sea into a river mouth where the water is fresh. What happens to the ship?

opts.t: It sits lower in the water, because it must displace a larger volume of the less dense fresh water
It sits higher, because fresh water is lighter
It stays at the same level, because the displaced volume depends only on the shape of the ship
It sits higher, because the river pushes harder

why: The weight of the ship is constant, so the weight of water displaced is constant. Fresh water has a lower density than sea water, so a greater volume is needed, and the hull sinks deeper. Ships carry load lines for this reason.
style: A prediction question about density change.

topic: Structures: Maximum load on a floating box
q: An open steel box is 2 m long, 1 m wide and 0.5 m deep and has a mass of 400 kg. Water density is 1,000 kg per cubic metre. What is the greatest extra mass it can carry in still fresh water without sinking below its rim?
why: Greatest displaced volume = 2 x 1 x 0.5 = 1 m^3, giving a maximum buoyant force equal to the weight of 1,000 kg of water. The box itself is 400 kg, so the extra mass is 1,000 - 400 = 600 kg.
style: A maximum-load question where you compare displaced water mass against the total mass.

q: Which statement best explains how an aeroplane wing produces lift?

opts.t: The engines push the plane straight up through the air
The air below the wing moves faster than the air above it
The wing is curved and tilted to the airflow, so it turns air downwards, and the pressure above the wing is lower than below
Hot air collects under the wing and floats it like a balloon

why: A wing pushes air downwards, so the air pushes the wing up (Newton's third law). The air over the curved top moves faster and its pressure is lower, giving an upward force. The thrust of the engine only drives the plane forwards.
style: A concept question that asks you to choose the correct physical explanation for lift.

q: The lift on a wing is proportional to the square of the airspeed. A light aircraft's wing gives lift equal to its weight at 60 m/s. At 30 m/s with the same wing angle, the lift will be about:

opts.t: The same as the aircraft's weight

why: Lift is proportional to v^2. Halving the speed from 60 to 30 gives (30/60)^2 = 1/4 of the lift. The aircraft would sink unless the pilot increases the angle or the speed, which is why take-off needs a minimum speed.
style: A ratio question with a squared dependence.

q: In a hydraulic jack, the small piston has an area of 5 square centimetres and the large piston has an area of 100 square centimetres. A force of 50 N is applied to the small piston. What force does the large piston exert?
why: Pressure is transmitted equally in the fluid: 50/5 = 10 N per cm^2. The large piston has 100 cm^2, so force = 10 x 100 = 1,000 N. Area ratio = 20, so the force is multiplied by 20.
style: A Pascal's law calculation with area ratio.

q: A hydraulic jack has a small piston of area 10 cm squared and a large piston of area 200 cm squared. The small piston is pushed down by 20 cm. How far does the large piston rise?
why: The liquid is incompressible, so the volume moved is equal: 10 x 20 = 200 cm^3. The large piston rises 200/200 = 1 cm. The force gain (x20) is paid for by a distance loss (1/20).
style: A volume-conservation question showing that distance is lost when force is gained.

q: Why does putting oil on a squeaky door hinge reduce friction?

opts.t: Oil makes the metal surfaces perfectly smooth
Oil makes the hinge lighter, so there is less weight to rub
A thin film of oil keeps the metal surfaces apart, so they slide over the film instead of catching on each other's rough points
Oil removes the force of gravity between the parts

why: Surfaces that look smooth have tiny bumps that lock together. A lubricant forms a layer that separates them, so sliding takes less force and there is less wear and heat.
style: A mechanism-explanation question about how lubricants work.

q: A 20 kg box rests on a level floor. The coefficient of friction between box and floor is 0.3. Taking g = 10 m/s^2, what is the smallest horizontal push that will make the box start to slide?
why: Normal force N = mg = 20 x 10 = 200 N. Limiting friction = coefficient x N = 0.3 x 200 = 60 N. A push of less than 60 N will not move the box.
style: A friction = mu x N calculation, with distractors from skipped steps.

q: A 12 V battery is connected across a single 4 ohm resistor. What current flows through the resistor?
why: Ohm's law says current = voltage / resistance = 12 / 4 = 3 A. Multiplying (48 A) is the common slip.
style: A one-step Ohm's law numerical with friendly numbers, often in a foundation-level paper.

q: Resistors of 3 ohm and 6 ohm are connected in series across a 9 V battery. What current flows in the circuit?
why: In series the resistances add: 3 + 6 = 9 ohm. Current = 9 V / 9 ohm = 1 A, and the same current flows through both resistors.
style: Asks for total resistance first, then current, testing whether you add resistances in series.

q: Two identical 6 ohm resistors are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance?
why: For two equal resistors in parallel, the combined value is half of one: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3, so R = 3 ohm. Parallel always gives less than the smallest branch.
style: Tests the idea that adding a parallel path lowers total resistance, often asked as a quick conceptual numerical.

q: What is the job of a fuse in a household circuit?

opts.t: It increases the current when the supply voltage drops
It stores charge so that the appliance never switches off
It changes alternating current into direct current
It melts and breaks the circuit when the current becomes too high

why: A fuse contains a thin wire that heats up and melts if the current exceeds a safe limit, stopping the flow before wires overheat and cause a fire.
style: A short recall question on safety devices, with options that mix up fuse, battery and rectifier.

q: A 5 A fuse protects a socket on a 230 V supply. Using power = voltage x current, which single appliance can run on this socket without blowing the fuse?
why: The highest safe power is 230 x 5 = 1150 W. A 1000 W heater draws about 4.3 A, which is under 5 A. The 1500 W, 2000 W and 3000 W appliances would draw about 6.5 A, 8.7 A and 13 A.
style: Combines P = VI with a safety limit, so you must work out the maximum power and compare each option.

q: In an old festival string of lights wired in series, the filament of one bulb breaks. What happens to the other bulbs?

opts.t: Only the bulbs next to it go off

why: A series circuit has only one path. A broken filament opens that path, so no current flows anywhere and every bulb goes off. This is why household wiring uses parallel branches.
style: A reasoning question that compares series and parallel wiring through a familiar festival-light story.

q: Which set contains only electrical insulators?
why: Rubber, dry wood and glass do not let charge move easily. The other sets include copper, steel or graphite, which are good conductors.
style: A simple classification question where one conductor hides among familiar insulators.

q: A wire has a resistance of 10 ohm. A second wire of the same material is twice as long and has twice the cross-section area. What is its resistance?
why: Resistance is proportional to length divided by area. Doubling the length doubles it; doubling the area halves it. The two effects cancel, so the resistance stays 10 ohm.
style: A proportional-reasoning question using R proportional to L/A, with two changes that cancel.

q: A 2 kW room heater runs for 3 hours. How many units (kWh) of electrical energy does it use?
why: Energy in kWh = power in kW x time in hours = 2 x 3 = 6 kWh. One unit on an electricity bill is 1 kWh.
style: A bill-style calculation: multiply power by time, being careful with units.

q: A motor takes in 500 J of electrical energy and gives out 400 J as useful work. What is its efficiency?
why: Efficiency = useful output / input x 100 = 400 / 500 x 100 = 80 percent. It can never be above 100 percent, which rules out 125 percent.
style: A direct efficiency calculation where one distractor is the upside-down fraction.

q: An old bulb of 60 W is replaced by an LED of 9 W. Both are lit for 5 hours. How much energy is saved?
why: The saving in power is 60 - 9 = 51 W. Over 5 hours that is 51 x 5 = 255 Wh = 0.255 kWh.
style: A multi-step comparison where you subtract powers, multiply by time and convert Wh to kWh.

q: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
why: Wind is replenished naturally and does not run out. Coal, natural gas and diesel come from fossil fuels that take millions of years to form.
style: A classification question on energy sources, common in school-level aptitude papers.

q: A rooftop solar panel produces direct current. Which device is needed to run an ordinary alternating-current household appliance from it?
why: An inverter converts direct current into alternating current. A rectifier does the opposite, a fuse only protects, and a transformer works only with alternating current.
style: Tests knowledge of what converts DC to AC in a solar system, with an opposite device as a trap.

q: A 12 V battery is rated 100 Ah. Ignoring losses, for how long can it supply a steady 120 W load?
why: Stored energy = 12 V x 100 Ah = 1200 Wh. Time = energy / power = 1200 / 120 = 10 hours.
style: A two-step energy question that turns amp-hours and volts into watt-hours before dividing by power.

q: Four identical 1.5 V cells are connected in parallel. Compared with one cell alone, what does this arrangement give?

opts.t: 6 V, with the same running time
3 V, with half the running time
The same 1.5 V, but it can supply current for longer
0.375 V, with four times the current

why: Cells in parallel share the load but keep the voltage of one cell. The total charge available is four times larger, so the supply lasts longer. Cells in series would add voltages instead.
style: Contrasts series and parallel cell arrangements, a favourite conceptual item.

q: A street light should switch on by itself when it becomes dark. Which sensor suits this job?
why: A light-dependent resistor changes its resistance with the light falling on it, so the circuit can detect darkness and switch the lamp on.
style: Matches a real-life automation task to the right sensor.

q: What does a microcontroller in a washing machine mainly do?

opts.t: Reads inputs and runs a stored program to control outputs
Supplies the electrical power to the drum motor
Stores clean water for each wash cycle
Turns the drum by its own moving parts

why: A microcontroller is a tiny programmable computer on a chip. It reads sensors and buttons, follows its program and switches outputs such as the motor and valves. Power and motion come from other parts.
style: Asks for the role of a controller in an everyday machine, separating decision-making from power and motion.

q: A room heater has a thermostat that switches it off when the room reaches a set temperature and on again when it cools. This is an example of what?
why: The thermostat senses the result (temperature) and uses it to decide whether to heat. Using the output to adjust the input is called feedback control.
style: Names the control idea behind a common appliance.

q: A robot arm uses a motor with a gear train that slows the arm down. What is the main benefit of this?

opts.t: The arm uses no electrical power
The arm moves faster than the motor
The arm gets more turning force (torque) at the joint

why: Gearing down trades speed for torque: a slower arm can lift heavier loads with the same motor. It does not remove power use or make the arm faster.
style: Tests the speed-versus-force trade-off in machines such as robot joints and bicycles.

q: What is the decimal value of the binary number 1011?
why: Place values from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8. So 1011 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.
style: A conversion question using place values of powers of two.

q: Which binary number equals 13 in decimal?
style: A conversion in the opposite direction, with near-miss patterns as distractors.

q: An algorithm starts with x = 2. It then repeats this step three times: replace x by (x times 2) plus 1. What is x at the end?
style: A dry-run question: carry out each step carefully and track the variable.

q: A security light must switch on only when it is dark AND movement is detected. Which logic gate matches this rule?
why: An AND gate gives output 1 only when both inputs are 1. An OR gate would switch the light on when either condition alone is true.
style: Translates a plain-language rule into a logic gate.

q: A program sets n = 1. While n is less than 20, it prints n and then adds 4 to n. How many numbers does it print?
why: The numbers printed are 1, 5, 9, 13 and 17. After 17 the value 21 is not less than 20, so the loop stops. That is 5 numbers.
style: A loop-tracing question where the stopping condition matters.

q: In a building fed from a rooftop tank, why is the water pressure at a ground floor tap higher than at a top floor tap?

opts.t: The column of water above the ground tap is taller
The ground floor pipe is always wider
Water gets heavier as it falls through the pipes
The tank pushes harder on lower floors

why: Pressure from a water column grows with its height. The ground floor tap has a much taller column of water above it than the top floor tap.
style: Links an everyday observation to the idea that pressure depends on depth or height of fluid.

q: Power is sent over long distances at very high voltage. What is the main reason?

opts.t: High voltage makes the wires thicker and stronger
The same power needs a smaller current, so less energy is lost as heat in the wires
High voltage makes the electricity travel faster than light
High voltage makes the power cost nothing to transmit

why: Power = voltage x current, so higher voltage means lower current for the same power. Heat loss in wires depends on current squared times resistance, so it falls sharply.
style: Asks why transmission uses high voltage, linking P = VI to heat loss.

q: When a photo is sent over the internet, it is broken into small pieces called packets. Why is this useful?

opts.t: Packets make the photo smaller than it was
Packets stop the photo from needing any network
Packets can travel by different routes and be put back together
Packets let the photo travel faster than the signal speed

why: Splitting data into packets lets a network share its links and route around busy or broken parts. The receiver reassembles the pieces in order.
style: A conceptual question on how networks move data.

q: Which manufacturing process involves pouring molten metal into a hollow shaped cavity and letting it solidify?
why: In casting, liquid metal fills a mould and cools into the shape of the cavity. Forging shapes hot metal by hammering, drilling cuts holes and welding joins parts.
style: A matching question linking process names to short descriptions.

q: Compared with carving a part out of a solid block, what is a main advantage of 3D printing?

opts.t: It builds the part layer by layer and wastes little material
It always makes parts stronger than carved ones
It works without any digital design file
It is always faster for every kind of part

why: 3D printing is additive: material is added only where the part needs it, so waste is low and complex shapes are possible. It is not always faster or stronger.
style: Tests the idea of additive versus subtractive manufacturing.

q: A shaft is specified as 20.00 mm with a tolerance of plus or minus 0.05 mm. Which measured diameter passes inspection?
why: Allowed range is 19.95 mm to 20.05 mm. 19.96 mm lies inside it; 19.93, 20.07 and 20.10 are outside.
style: A quality-check question: find the limits from the tolerance, then test each value.

topic: Maths: properties of odd and even numbers
q: Which statement is always true for any two odd whole numbers?
why: Odd x odd is always odd (for example 3 x 5 = 15). The sum and difference of two odd numbers are even, so those statements fail.
style: A parity question that can be settled by testing a few examples.

q: What is the smallest number greater than 1 that leaves remainder 1 when divided by each of 2, 3, 4 and 5?
why: The number minus 1 must be a multiple of 2, 3, 4 and 5. Their LCM is 60, so the number is 60 + 1 = 61. 31 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4.
style: A number-theory reasoning item: subtract the common remainder and use the LCM.

q: How many different positive whole-number factors does 36 have?
why: The factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36, which is 9. Square numbers have an odd number of factors.
style: Factor counting, sometimes done through prime factorisation.

q: Which of these fractions is the largest: 5/8, 3/5, 7/12, 2/3?
why: As decimals they are about 0.625, 0.6, 0.583 and 0.667. So 2/3 is the largest.
style: Ordering fractions by converting to a common form.

q: A tank is 3/5 full. Then one third of the water in it is used. What fraction of the whole tank is still filled?
why: Two thirds of the water remains: 3/5 x 2/3 = 6/15 = 2/5 of the tank.
style: A story using a fraction of a fraction, where the base changes.

q: What is 0.4 multiplied by 0.05?
why: 4 x 5 = 20, and there are three decimal places in total (one + two), so the answer is 0.020 = 0.02.
style: Decimal placement is the main trap in such a question.

q: Red and white paint are mixed in the ratio 2 : 3. How much white paint is needed to make 20 litres of the mixture?
why: The ratio has 2 + 3 = 5 parts, so 1 part = 4 litres. White is 3 parts = 12 litres.
style: Share a total in a given ratio.

q: Six workers can build a wall in 10 days. If all workers work at the same pace, how many days will 15 workers take?
why: The job is 6 x 10 = 60 worker-days. With 15 workers, 60 / 15 = 4 days. More workers means fewer days.
style: Tests whether you notice that this is inverse, not direct, proportion.

q: The ratio of boys to girls in a class is 3 : 2. When 10 more girls join, the number of girls equals the number of boys. How many students were in the class originally?
why: Let boys = 3k and girls = 2k. Then 2k + 10 = 3k, so k = 10. The class had 30 + 20 = 50 students.
style: A ratio problem that needs a variable for the common multiple and an equation.

q: The sum of three consecutive whole numbers is 72. What is the largest of the three?
why: The middle number is 72 / 3 = 24, so the numbers are 23, 24 and 25. The largest is 25.
style: Uses the mean of consecutive numbers as a shortcut.

q: I think of a number, double it and subtract 7. The result is 15. What was my number?
why: Work backwards: 15 + 7 = 22, then 22 / 2 = 11. Check: 2 x 11 - 7 = 15.
style: A reverse-operations puzzle that is really a one-step equation.

q: Two numbers x and y satisfy x + y = 10 and x - y = 4. What is the value of x times y?
why: Adding the equations gives 2x = 14, so x = 7 and y = 3. Then xy = 21.
style: A pair of equations solved by adding or subtracting them.

q: The sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, ... continues with a constant step. What is its 10th term?
why: The step is 3, so the nth term is 5 + 3(n - 1) = 3n + 2. For n = 10 this gives 32.
style: Finding a general term from a pattern.

q: In a triangle ABC, angle A is 50 degrees and angle B is 65 degrees. What is the exterior angle at C, formed by extending side BC?
why: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: 50 + 65 = 115. Check: angle C is 65, and 180 - 65 = 115.
style: Applies the exterior angle property of a triangle.

q: A square has a perimeter of 36 cm. What is its area?
why: Each side is 36 / 4 = 9 cm, so the area is 9 x 9 = 81 square cm.
style: Moves from perimeter to side to area.

q: A rectangular floor measures 8 m by 6 m. It is covered with square tiles of side 50 cm, with no gaps. How many tiles are needed?
why: Floor area = 48 square m. Each tile is 0.5 m x 0.5 m = 0.25 square m. So 48 / 0.25 = 192 tiles.
style: A unit-conversion trap: tile size is in cm while the floor is in m.

q: Each side of a square is doubled. What happens to its area?

opts.t: It becomes eight times as large
It becomes four times as large

why: Area depends on side squared. Doubling the side gives 2 x 2 = 4 times the area.
style: Tests the idea that area scales with the square of the scale factor.

q: A shop sold tickets on five days: Monday 40, Tuesday 55, Wednesday 35, Thursday 60, Friday 60. What was the mean number sold per day?
why: The total is 40 + 55 + 35 + 60 + 60 = 250. Dividing by 5 days gives 50.
style: Reads values from a small table and finds the mean.

q: The marks of eight students are 4, 7, 7, 9, 10, 12, 12 and 12. What is the mode minus the median?
why: The mode (most frequent) is 12. The median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values: (9 + 10) / 2 = 9.5. So 12 - 9.5 = 2.5.
style: Combines two statistics that students often confuse.

q: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green balls. One ball is picked at random. What is the probability that it is not blue?
why: There are 10 balls and 5 are not blue (3 + 2). So the probability is 5/10 = 1/2.
style: A basic probability question using the complement idea.

q: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
why: The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT. Three of them have at least one head, so the probability is 3/4.
style: List all outcomes and count the favourable ones.

q: How many two-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3 and 4 if no digit is used twice in a number?
why: There are 4 choices for the tens digit and then 3 for the units digit: 4 x 3 = 12.
style: The multiplication principle of counting.

q: Six people at a meeting each shake hands once with every other person. How many handshakes take place?
why: Each person shakes hands with 5 others, giving 6 x 5 = 30, but every handshake is counted twice. So 30 / 2 = 15.
style: A classic counting question about avoiding double counting.

q: Which is the best estimate of 49.7 multiplied by 20.1?
why: Round to 50 x 20 = 1000. The exact value is close to 999, so 1000 is the best estimate.
style: Rounding to friendly numbers to check the size of an answer.

q: In a traditional school paint box, which three colours are the primary colours, because they cannot be made by mixing other paints?
why: Primary paints cannot be mixed from other paints, but mixing them gives most other colours.
style: The exam shows a colour situation and asks which colour idea explains it.

q: You mix blue paint with yellow paint in equal amounts. Which colour do you get?
why: Blue and yellow are primaries, and together they make the secondary colour green.
style: The exam shows a colour situation and asks which colour idea explains it.

q: On the traditional paint colour wheel, which colour sits directly opposite blue and is called its complementary colour?
why: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the wheel and look strong and lively side by side. Blue and orange are such a pair.
style: The exam shows a colour situation and asks which colour idea explains it.

q: Which set contains only warm colours, the kind that remind us of fire and sunshine?
why: Reds, oranges and yellows feel warm. Blues, greens and violets feel cool.
style: The exam shows a colour situation and asks which colour idea explains it.

q: A phone screen makes colours from light. When red light and green light overlap on the screen, what colour do you see?
why: Light mixes by adding, which is the opposite of paint. Red light plus green light gives yellow, and all three light primaries together give white.
style: The exam shows a colour situation and asks which colour idea explains it.

q: A designer adds white to red paint to make a lighter pink. What is a lighter version of a colour called?
why: Adding white makes a tint, and adding black makes a shade.
style: The exam shows a colour situation and asks which colour idea explains it.

q: Which choice is easiest to read from far away on a warning sign?

opts.t: Light grey letters on a white background
Yellow letters on a white background
Black letters on a bright yellow background
Pale blue letters on a light green background

why: Strong contrast between letters and background, like black on yellow, makes a message easy to see from a distance.
style: The exam shows a colour situation and asks which colour idea explains it.

q: Which capital letter has a vertical line of symmetry, so its left half mirrors its right half?
why: If you fold the letter A down the middle, the two halves match. F, G and R do not match when folded this way.
style: The exam shows a shape, pattern or layout described in words and asks which idea or answer fits.

q: Which shape looks exactly the same after a quarter turn (90 degrees) about its centre?

opts.t: A rectangle longer than it is wide

why: A square has four equal sides and fits onto itself at every quarter turn. The triangle needs a turn of 120 degrees, and the others do not fit at 90 degrees.
style: The exam shows a shape, pattern or layout described in words and asks which idea or answer fits.

q: A border repeats in this order: circle, circle, square, circle, circle, square, circle. What comes next?
why: The unit is circle, circle, square. The row has finished two units and started a third with one circle, so the second circle of that unit comes next.
style: The exam shows a shape, pattern or layout described in words and asks which idea or answer fits.

q: A poster has one large dark heavy shape on its left. The designer wants balance without a mirror copy. What can she do?

opts.t: Leave the right side completely empty
Add another large dark shape right on top of the first
Add smaller shapes or bright accents on the right to share the visual weight
Move the heavy shape to a corner and leave the rest blank

why: Balance does not need a mirror image. Several small or bright shapes can weigh as much as one big dark shape, giving asymmetric balance.
style: The exam shows a shape, pattern or layout described in words and asks which idea or answer fits.

q: On a notice board, which change makes a title stand out most from the text below it?

opts.t: Write it in the same size and style as the text
Make it smaller than the body text
Use the same weight and colour as the text
Make it much larger and bolder than the other text

why: Contrast in size and weight tells the eye what to read first.
style: The exam shows a shape, pattern or layout described in words and asks which idea or answer fits.

q: Which flat pattern of squares can be folded to make an open box with a base and four sides but no lid?

opts.t: A plus-shaped cross of five squares
A straight row of five squares
A 2 by 2 block of four squares
An L-shape made of three squares

why: A centre square for the base and four squares around it fold up as the sides. A line of squares cannot wrap around to make walls.
style: The exam shows a shape, pattern or layout described in words and asks which idea or answer fits.

q: Why are the handles of cooking pans usually made of wood or plastic instead of metal?

opts.t: They are stronger than any metal
They conduct heat poorly, so they stay cooler to hold
They help the pan heat up faster
They stop the food from sticking

why: Wood and plastic do not carry heat well, so the cook can hold the pan safely.
style: The exam shows an everyday object and asks why it was made that way.

q: A kettle has a narrow spout that slopes downward. What is the main reason for this shape?

opts.t: It makes the water boil faster
It keeps all the steam inside the kettle
It guides the water into a thin, controlled stream
It makes the kettle lighter to carry

why: A narrow spout lets the user pour exactly where they want, with little spilling.
style: The exam shows an everyday object and asks why it was made that way.

q: A door has a smooth flat metal plate and no handle. What is this design telling you to do?
why: A flat plate has nothing to hold, so it invites a push. A bar or loop invites a pull. This hint from an object's shape is called an affordance.
style: The exam shows an everyday object and asks why it was made that way.

q: Why is an emergency stop button on a machine large, red and shaped like a mushroom?

opts.t: It can be found and hit quickly with a palm, even in panic
