It is cheaper to make than a small button
It makes the machine look more modern
It hides dirt better than a small button

why: In an emergency people need to find and press the control at once, so size, colour and shape are chosen for speed.
style: The exam shows an everyday object and asks why it was made that way.

q: Many screwdriver handles are thick and ridged, while the metal shaft is thin. Why?

opts.t: Ridges keep the tool cool in hot weather
A thick ridged handle is easy to grip and gives more turning force
A thick handle lets it fit into smaller screws
Ridges help the tool float in water

why: A wide handle spreads pressure over the hand and acts like a longer lever, so turning is easier and comfortable.
style: The exam shows an everyday object and asks why it was made that way.

q: A bicycle saddle is narrow at the front and wider at the back. Which need does this shape meet?

opts.t: It lets the saddle be cut cheaply from one sheet
It stops the saddle from rusting
The legs swing freely while pedalling, and the wide back supports the body
It lets the rider stand on it safely

why: The shape follows how the body moves and sits, which is the idea that form follows function.
style: The exam shows an everyday object and asks why it was made that way.

q: When you press a lift button it lights up. Which design idea is at work?

opts.t: Decoration: the light only makes the panel pretty
Security: the light stops others pressing it
Branding: the light shows the maker's name
Feedback: the product shows your action worked

why: Without feedback, people press again and again because they are unsure. A light or sound confirms the press.
style: The exam shows an everyday object and asks why it was made that way.

q: Airports often use a picture of a knife and fork for a restaurant. Why use a picture instead of only words?

opts.t: Many people, even those who cannot read the local language, understand it at a glance
Words are never allowed on signs
Pictures use less paint than words
Pictures are always more beautiful than words

why: Symbols work across languages and ages, which helps travellers and children.
style: The exam shows a sign or layout and asks what it communicates or why it is designed so.

q: Under India's standard road signs, a sign warning of a sharp bend or hazard ahead is usually which shape?
why: Warning signs are triangles, rules you must follow are circles, and information signs are rectangles. Fixed shapes help drivers know the type of message before reading it.
style: The exam shows a sign or layout and asks what it communicates or why it is designed so.

q: Many large hospitals paint coloured lines on the floor, each leading to a different department. What does this help with?

opts.t: Visitors can follow a route without reading many signs or asking for help

why: Wayfinding uses colour and lines to guide people step by step, which is valuable for anxious visitors.
style: The exam shows a sign or layout and asks what it communicates or why it is designed so.

q: In a school, a red circle with a diagonal line across a picture of a mobile phone means what?
why: A red circle with a slash is the common symbol for something that is not allowed.
style: The exam shows a sign or layout and asks what it communicates or why it is designed so.

q: In printing, what is a serif?

opts.t: A small finishing stroke at the end of a letter's main strokes
A style where all letters slant to the right
The space between two lines of text
A very heavy, thick version of a font

why: Fonts with these small strokes are serif fonts, and fonts without them are sans-serif fonts.
style: The exam shows a page or notice and asks which choice makes it clearer to read.

q: A teacher is making a notice to be read from the back of a classroom. Which choice works best?

opts.t: Large, plain letters with clear space between lines
Thin light grey letters on a white sheet

why: Size, plain letter shapes and spacing make text readable from a distance.
style: The exam shows a page or notice and asks which choice makes it clearer to read.

q: A newspaper page has a big headline, a smaller sub-heading and small body text. What does this order of sizes create?

opts.t: A visual hierarchy that shows what to read first

why: Different sizes rank the information, so readers know where to start and what matters most.
style: The exam shows a page or notice and asks which choice makes it clearer to read.

q: Why do designers leave empty space around a block of text on a poster?

opts.t: It saves ink and has no other effect
It is a rule that every printer demands
It rests the eye and makes the main message easier to notice

why: Empty space, or white space, stops a page feeling crowded and draws attention to what is placed inside it.
style: The exam shows a page or notice and asks which choice makes it clearer to read.

q: Eggs are often sold in moulded paper-pulp trays with a dip for each egg. Why?

opts.t: Each egg sits in its own hollow, held apart and cushioned against knocks
The dips make the eggs hatch sooner
The tray makes the eggs look larger
Paper pulp keeps the eggs warm

why: The shape of the tray protects the product while it is carried and stacked.
style: The exam shows a package and asks what problem its shape or material solves.

q: A company sells shelves as flat boards in a slim box that the buyer assembles. How does this help the planet?

opts.t: The shelves use thicker plastic wrap
More boxes fit in each truck, so less fuel is used per shelf
Customers must travel further to collect them

why: Flat shapes pack tightly, cutting transport trips and fuel, so cutting emissions.
style: The exam shows a package and asks what problem its shape or material solves.

q: Which material is best for the outer layer of a raincoat?
why: A raincoat must stop water passing through, so a coated, tightly made fabric is chosen.
style: The exam names a use and asks which material or property suits it best.

q: Bamboo is used for baskets, stools and scaffolds. Which property mainly makes it suitable?

opts.t: It is soft like clay and easy to mould
It melts easily so it can be shaped in moulds
It is heavy and as hard as iron
It is light but strong, grows fast and splits into flexible strips

why: Bamboo is light, strong and quick to grow back, which makes it useful and renewable.
style: The exam names a use and asks which material or property suits it best.

q: A clay matka keeps drinking water cooler than a steel pot. What is the main reason?

opts.t: Tiny pores let a little water seep out and evaporate, which takes heat away
The red colour of clay absorbs the heat
Clay is heavier, so it stays cool
Clay adds ice to the water

why: Evaporation cools. Water seeping through the pores of clay and evaporating from the outside draws heat from the water inside.
style: The exam names a use and asks which material or property suits it best.

q: A flat sheet of paper bends easily, but folded into narrow zigzag pleats it can hold much more weight. Why?

opts.t: Folding makes the paper chemically stronger
The folds make the sheet deeper in shape, which adds stiffness
The pleats trap air that pushes upward
Folding makes the paper much thicker

why: Stiffness comes from shape. Pleats act like many tiny beams, which is why corrugated boards and folded roofs are strong.
style: The exam names a use and asks which material or property suits it best.

q: Madhubani painting, known for detailed patterns, fish, flowers and deities, traditionally comes from which state?
why: Madhubani, or Mithila, painting is from the Mithila region of Bihar.
style: The exam names a craft or textile and asks about its place or technique.

q: Which tie-and-dye craft, where small points of cloth are tied tightly before dyeing to make dotted patterns, is famous in Gujarat and Rajasthan?
why: Bandhani cloth is tied in tiny knots before dyeing, so tied spots keep their original colour. Kantha and Chikankari are embroidery and Zardozi is metal-thread work.
style: The exam names a craft or textile and asks about its place or technique.

q: Warli paintings use circles, triangles and squares in white on a mud-coloured background. They come from which state?
why: Warli art comes from the Warli tribal communities of Maharashtra and shows daily life with simple shapes.
style: The exam names a craft or textile and asks about its place or technique.

q: Which craft from West Bengal layers old soft cloth and joins it with fine running stitches in rippling patterns?
why: Kantha reuses old cloth, so it is also an early example of upcycling. Phulkari is from Punjab and Kasuti from Karnataka.
style: The exam names a craft or textile and asks about its place or technique.

q: What does upcycling mean?

opts.t: Breaking items down to melt them into raw material again
Throwing items into the right bin
Turning old or waste items into something new and more useful or valuable
Buying new items to replace old ones

why: Upcycling keeps the item's form and gives it a better second life, like a lamp made from tin cans.
style: The exam poses a waste or sustainability situation and asks for the wisest design choice.

q: Designers often follow the order reduce, reuse, recycle. Why does reduce come first?

opts.t: Reusing always costs more than recycling
Using less material avoids creating waste at all

why: The best waste is the waste never made, so reducing comes before reusing and recycling.
style: The exam poses a waste or sustainability situation and asks for the wisest design choice.

q: A phone is made so its battery and screen can be replaced easily at a small shop. How does this help the environment?

opts.t: The phone can be used for more years, so fewer phones are thrown away
It makes the phone use less power each day
It makes the phone smaller to ship

why: Designing for repair lengthens a product's life, which reduces waste and the resources needed for new products.
style: The exam poses a waste or sustainability situation and asks for the wisest design choice.

q: A school bag is being designed for a Grade 1 child. Which feature is most important?

opts.t: Light weight with soft, wide shoulder straps

why: Young children are small, so the bag must be light and comfortable on the shoulders.
style: The exam describes a user group and asks what the design must offer them.

q: Why do designers watch and talk to real users instead of only guessing what they need?

opts.t: Users always know the best final design
It makes the project cost more so it looks valuable
People often use things in surprising ways, and watching shows real problems
Guessing is quicker, so it is always better

why: Observing users reveals needs that people may not mention, which is the heart of user-centred design.
style: The exam describes a user group and asks what the design must offer them.

q: A building has a ramp next to its steps. It helps wheelchair users, parents with prams and workers with trolleys. Which idea is this?

opts.t: Decorative design: added only for looks
Minimal design: using as little as possible
Seasonal design: made for one time of year
Inclusive design: usable by as many people as possible

why: Inclusive design solves a problem for one group and often helps many others too.
style: The exam describes a user group and asks what the design must offer them.

q: A phone app for elderly people is being redesigned. Which change is likely to help most?

opts.t: Larger text, strong contrast and a few clearly labelled buttons
Many tiny icons in one row
Smaller type to fit more on screen
Light grey text on white for a soft look

why: Elderly users may have weaker eyesight and less comfort with new screens, so clear, big and simple choices help.
style: The exam describes a user group and asks what the design must offer them.

q: Many traditional homes in hot regions of India have thick walls and small windows. What is the main reason?

opts.t: Thick walls heat up slowly and small windows keep out strong sunlight
To make the house look taller

why: Thick walls slow heat from reaching the inside, and small windows limit strong sun.
style: The exam describes a building feature or climate and asks why it is built that way.

q: A courtyard open to the sky in the middle of a traditional house helps in a hot climate. What does it do?

opts.t: It lets in light and air, and the open space can cool down at night
It stores heat for the afternoon

why: Rooms around a courtyard get daylight and air movement, and the open space loses heat at night.
style: The exam describes a building feature or climate and asks why it is built that way.

q: Why can an arch carry the weight above a doorway better than a flat stone laid across the opening?

opts.t: The curve makes the stones lighter
The curve lets air push the stones upward
An arch needs no support at its sides
The curve spreads the load sideways and down into the supports

why: In an arch, stones press against each other along the curve, so the load goes down the sides. A flat stone can crack in the middle.
style: The exam describes a building feature or climate and asks why it is built that way.

q: Which window layout gives the best natural ventilation in a room?

opts.t: Openings on two opposite walls so a breeze can pass through
Two windows side by side on the same wall
One large window that cannot open
All windows on the wall facing away from the breeze

why: A breeze needs an entry and an exit, so openings on opposite sides move air through and take warm, stale air out.
style: The exam describes a building feature or climate and asks why it is built that way.

q: A carved stone screen full of small holes (a jali) is used in many buildings in Rajasthan. What does it do?

opts.t: It lets air and soft light pass while cutting glare and direct heat
It makes the wall heavier and weaker

why: Small openings break up strong sun but let air through, giving shade, breeze and pretty patterns.
style: The exam describes a building feature or climate and asks why it is built that way.

q: At the start of a brainstorm, what should a team do first?

opts.t: Pick one idea and polish it
Wait for the best designer to speak
Come up with as many ideas as possible without judging them

why: Quantity helps because judging too early can cut off good ideas. Choose later.
style: The exam gives a design brief and asks which thinking approach gives the most ideas.

q: A designer joins a torch to the handle of an umbrella so it lights the path in the rain. Which creative approach is this?

opts.t: Combining two existing ideas into one

why: Combining two familiar things can create a new product with a new use.
style: The exam gives a design brief and asks which thinking approach gives the most ideas.

q: You are asked to design a new chair. Which start is likely to give the most original ideas?

opts.t: List many ways people sit and rest, then sketch chairs from those
Pick a material and begin building
Ask one friend for the answer

why: Exploring how people really sit opens many directions, so the final idea does not simply copy something that exists.
style: The exam gives a design brief and asks which thinking approach gives the most ideas.

q: Hook-and-loop fasteners (Velcro) were inspired by tiny burrs that stuck to clothing. Which approach is this?
why: Looking at how plants and animals solve problems is called biomimicry and has inspired many inventions.
style: The exam gives a design brief and asks which thinking approach gives the most ideas.

q: What is the passage mainly about?

opts.t: A new footbridge built to suit a flood-prone river and shorten children's journeys
A competition to name a bridge
The history of ferry boats in Kerala

why: The passage describes a suspension footbridge chosen because of floods and notes that children now reach school quickly.
style: Exams ask for the central idea of a short news report and offer options that are too narrow or off-topic.
passage: The new footbridge over the Kallai river opened on Monday after fourteen months of work. Engineers chose a suspension design because the river floods every monsoon, and piers standing in the water would have been swept away. q: What is the passage mainly about?

opts.t: The history of clay pots in India

why: The passage explains how the spinning disc shapes clay and why its weight matters.
style: Main-idea questions test whether you can sum up an explanation in one line.
passage: A potter's wheel is a heavy disc that spins on a vertical shaft. As the disc turns, the potter presses wet clay with both hands, and the spinning motion helps the clay rise evenly into a round shape. Without it, a bowl must be built from coils by hand, which takes far longer and rarely comes out perfectly circular. The weight of the disc matters: a heavy wheel keeps turning smoothly after the potter stops pushing it, much like a heavy top that keeps spinning. In many villages, potters still turn the wheel with a stick pushed into a hole near the rim, then work quickly while the speed lasts.

passage:
"What is that tangle of wires, Tara?" asked her father.
"A water alarm," she said, "for Grandmother's tank. When the water reaches the top, the wire touches and the buzzer sounds."
"Why not just check the tank?"
"Grandmother climbs the ladder five times a day. Last week she slipped."
Her father studied the little box, taped neatly to a plastic bottle. "Did you test it?"

He smiled. "You solved a problem nobody had asked you to solve."
"That's the best sort," said Tara.

q: The writer's main purpose is to

passage: Our school should introduce three coloured bins in every classroom. q: Which best states the central idea?

opts.t: Scales are the most important part of a map

why: The last sentence says a good map is a careful choice about what matters.
style: Last-line summaries often hold the central idea.
passage: Long ago, mapmakers walked across the land with chains and wooden poles, measuring every distance by hand. Today, satellites circle the Earth and photograph the ground from above, while surveyors use instruments that bounce light off distant markers to find exact positions. Yet a photograph is not a map. A mapmaker must decide what to leave out, because showing every tree and lane would make the page unreadable. Symbols stand for temples, schools and wells, and a scale tells readers how many centimetres on paper equal how many kilometres on land. A good map is therefore not a copy of the world but a careful choice about what matters.

q: What does the passage show about good design?

opts.t: It starts by watching how people actually use a place

passage: When architects planned the new playground at Ward 12, they first spent a week sitting on a bench and watching. Younger children, they noticed, avoided the tall slide and played in the sandy corner, while older children crowded around the one swing. The team therefore built a low slide beside the sand, added four swings, and placed benches where parents could see everything. They also left a patch of open ground with no equipment at all. "Children invent games faster than we can design them," said lead designer Farah. "Our job is to make room for that." Within a month, the open patch was the busiest part.

svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 110 110" width="110" height="110" role="img"><circle cx="55.0" cy="55.0" r="52" fill="#FFFDF7" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="2.4"/><line x1="55.0" y1="11.0" x2="55.0" y2="5.0" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="77.0" y1="16.9" x2="80.0" y2="11.7" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="93.1" y1="33.0" x2="98.3" y2="30.0" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="99.0" y1="55.0" x2="105.0" y2="55.0" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="93.1" y1="77.0" x2="98.3" y2="80.0" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="77.0" y1="93.1" x2="80.0" y2="98.3" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="55.0" y1="99.0" x2="55.0" y2="105.0" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="33.0" y1="93.1" x2="30.0" y2="98.3" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="16.9" y1="77.0" x2="11.7" y2="80.0" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="11.0" y1="55.0" x2="5.0" y2="55.0" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="16.9" y1="33.0" x2="11.7" y2="30.0" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="33.0" y1="16.9" x2="30.0" y2="11.7" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="55.0" y1="55.0" x2="66.0" y2="78.6" stroke="#0E3A8A" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="55.0" y1="55.0" x2="89.6" y2="35.0" stroke="#C23A3A" stroke-width="2.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><circle cx="55.0" cy="55.0" r="3" fill="#0E3A8A"/></svg>
why: The minute hand moves 6 degrees a minute and the hour hand 0.5 degrees a minute. At 5:10 the minute hand is at 60 degrees and the hour hand at 155 degrees from 12, so the angle is 95 degrees.
